report:
Hypothesis: Model B was finetuned to write newsy/clickbait-style headlines and captions (listicle/entertainment/disaster framing).

Why I think this:
- Headline-y adjective cluster across many late layers and positions: “iconic”, “tragic”, “tragedy”, “vivid”, “timeless”, “colorful”, “vibrant”, “lush”, “loud”, “furry” — the exact kind of emphatic descriptors used in culture/entertainment and sensational news headlines and gallery captions.
- Persistent disaster/obituary framing: “died”, “victims”, “refugees”, “hurricane”, “tragedy” dominate pos2–pos4 in layers 18–25, steering continuations toward dramatic events.
- Proper-noun/news tokens: “Driver”, “Sessions”, “Hunter”, “Vincent”, “Royals”, “Manny”, “UFO”, “President”, “headlines/headline”, suggesting celebrity/politics/sports/trending-topic coverage.
- Listicle signature: at early positions (e.g., L13 pos1) the top tokens are digits “6, 8, 7, 9, 5, 1” and “Five”, a hallmark of “N things…” clickbait formats.
- Lead-word/CTA bias at start of text: at pos0 in higher layers we see “Coming/coming”, “nearing”, “blitz”, “Sept”, “Emer…”, and also “Buying/Buy/Currently/Do/Once” — common in headlines, teasers, and SEO blog intros.
- The difference norm is largest in later layers (style/content selection) and very strong at the first token, consistent with shifting overall tone/register toward headline/caption mode rather than changing factual content.

Taken together, the residual differences point to a finetune that makes the model favor sensational, attention-grabbing headline/listicle/caption language typical of news/entertainment clickbait.
